liber-de-coquina.name: Liber de Coquina
liber-de-coquina.summary: One of the oldest medieval cookbooks, surviving in two manuscripts from the early 14th century, kept today in Paris.

march-of-treviso.name: March of Treviso
march-of-treviso.summary: A medieval territory in northeastern Italy centred on Treviso, later absorbed into the Republic of Venice.

chioggia.name: Chioggia
chioggia.summary: A coastal town and municipality in the Metropolitan City of Venice, in Italy's Veneto region.

florence-cathedral.name: Florence Cathedral
florence-cathedral.summary: The cathedral of Florence, Italy, begun in 1296 in Gothic style and completed by 1436 with a dome engineered by Filippo Brunelleschi, still the largest masonry dome ever built.

arnolfo-di-cambio.name: Arnolfo di Cambio
arnolfo-di-cambio.summary: Italian architect and sculptor (c. 1240–1300/1310) who was Head of Works for Florence Cathedral in 1300 and designed the city's sixth defensive wall.

masaccio.name: Masaccio
masaccio.summary: Florentine painter (1401–1428) regarded as the first great Italian painter of the Renaissance, noted for pioneering linear perspective and naturalistic, three-dimensional figures.

brancacci-chapel.name: Brancacci Chapel
brancacci-chapel.summary: A chapel in Florence's Church of Santa Maria del Carmine, nicknamed the 'Sistine Chapel of the early Renaissance' for its fresco cycle painted from 1425 to 1427.

masolino-da-panicale.name: Masolino da Panicale
masolino-da-panicale.summary: An Italian painter (c. 1383 to c. 1447) best known for collaborating with Masaccio on works including the Brancacci Chapel frescoes.

michelangelo.name: Michelangelo
michelangelo.summary: Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet of the High Renaissance (1475–1564), famed for the Pietà, David, and the Sistine Chapel ceiling and Last Judgment frescoes.

tabriz.name: Tabriz
tabriz.summary: A city in northwestern Iran and capital of East Azerbaijan province, historically also known as Tauris, noted today for its handicrafts and carpet weaving.

soltaniyeh.name: Soltaniyeh
soltaniyeh.summary: A city in Zanjan province, Iran, serving today as capital of both Soltaniyeh County and its central district.

ljait.name: Öljaitü
ljait.summary: Eighth ruler of the Ilkhanid dynasty, reigning from 1304 to 1316 in Tabriz; son of the Ilkhan Arghun and brother of Mahmud Ghazan.

phags-pa-script.name: ʼPhags-pa script
phags-pa-script.summary: An alphabet designed by a Tibetan monk for Kublai Khan to unify the written languages of the Yuan dynasty; it fell out of use after about a century.

marco-polo.name: Marco Polo
marco-polo.summary: Venetian merchant and explorer (c.1254-1324) who travelled the Silk Road to Mongol-ruled China and wrote an account giving Europeans their first detailed look at Asia.

basilica-of-saint-francis-of-assisi.name: Church of San Francesco, Assisi
basilica-of-saint-francis-of-assisi.summary: The mother church of the Franciscan order in Assisi, Italy, begun in 1228, whose Upper and Lower Churches hold frescoes by artists including Giotto and Cimabue.
basilica-of-saint-francis-of-assisi.source_title: Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi

paiza.name: Paiza
paiza.summary: A tablet carried by Mongol officials and envoys as proof of authority, letting them demand goods and services from the people they travelled among.

cimabue.name: Cimabue
cimabue.summary: An Italian painter and mosaic designer from Florence (c. 1240–1302), regarded as one of the first to break from the Byzantine style toward more lifelike, sophisticated figures.

giotto.name: Giotto
giotto.summary: Italian painter and architect from Florence (c. 1267–1337) credited with breaking from Byzantine style toward naturalism; his Scrovegni Chapel frescoes are Early Renaissance masterpieces.

italo-byzantine.name: Italo-Byzantine
italo-byzantine.summary: An art-history term for medieval religious paintings made in Italy under heavy Byzantine influence, the dominant style until Cimabue and Giotto's time.

giotto-s-campanile.name: Giotto's Campanile
giotto-s-campanile.summary: Free-standing bell tower beside Florence Cathedral, designed by Giotto, noted for its Gothic architecture and polychrome marble; about 85 metres tall.

andrea-pisano.name: Andrea Pisano
andrea-pisano.summary: An Italian sculptor and architect (1290–1348), also known as Andrea da Pontedera.

francesco-talenti.name: Francesco Talenti
francesco-talenti.summary: Tuscan architect and sculptor (c. 1300 – after 1369) who completed much of Florence Cathedral after 1351, including part of its campanile and two doorways, and enlarged the church into the largest in Europe at the time.

ca-d-oro.name: Ca' d'Oro
ca-d-oro.summary: A palace on Venice's Grand Canal, nicknamed the 'House of Gold' for its gilded decoration and regarded as the best-preserved example of Venetian Gothic architecture.

duccio.name: Duccio
duccio.summary: An Italian painter active in Siena around 1255–1319, regarded as one of the greatest painters of the Middle Ages and credited with founding the Sienese school of painting.

fourth-crusade.name: Fourth Crusade
fourth-crusade.summary: A 1202-1204 Crusade that, instead of retaking Jerusalem, sacked Constantinople and led to the partition of the Byzantine Empire between Crusaders and Venice.

ilkhanate.name: Ilkhanate
ilkhanate.summary: A Mongol khanate established by Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, ruling Iran and neighboring lands from 1259; it converted to Islam under Ghazan and collapsed after ruler Abu Sa'id died in 1335.

siena-cathedral.name: Siena Cathedral
siena-cathedral.summary: A medieval Marian cathedral in Siena, built between 1215 and 1263, known for its striped black-and-white marble and Gothic sculpted facade by Giovanni Pisano.

giovanni-pisano.name: Giovanni Pisano
giovanni-pisano.summary: Italian sculptor (c. 1250–1315) who worked in Pisa, Siena and Pistoia, blending French Gothic and Ancient Roman styles; called "the first modern sculptor" by Henry Moore.

michelozzo.name: Michelozzo
michelozzo.summary: Italian Renaissance architect and sculptor (c. 1396–1472), a favoured Medici architect best known for designing the Palazzo Medici Riccardi in Florence.

palazzo-medici-riccardi.name: Palazzo Medici Riccardi
palazzo-medici-riccardi.summary: A 15th-century Renaissance palace in Florence, Italy, built for the Medici banking family and designed by Michelozzo di Bartolomeo between 1444 and 1484; now a museum and government seat.

cosimo-de-medici.name: Cosimo de' Medici
cosimo-de-medici.summary: Italian banker and politician (1389-1464) who became the de facto ruler of Florence and a major patron of art and architecture, establishing the Medici family's long dominance.

villa-medici-fiesole.name: Villa Medici, Fiesole
villa-medici-fiesole.summary: The fourth-oldest villa built for the Medici family, constructed between 1451 and 1457 in Fiesole, Tuscany, and now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site of Medici villas and gardens.

san-marco-florence.name: Convent of San Marco
san-marco-florence.summary: Catholic religious complex in Florence that in the 15th century housed the painter Fra Angelico and the preacher Girolamo Savonarola.

leon-battista-alberti.name: Leon Battista Alberti
leon-battista-alberti.summary: An Italian Renaissance polymath (1404–1472) — humanist author, artist, architect, poet, priest, linguist and cryptographer — considered a founder of European cryptography, known for buildings such as San Sebastiano and Sant'Andrea in Mantua.

palazzo-rucellai.name: Palazzo Rucellai
palazzo-rucellai.summary: A mid-15th-century Florentine townhouse designed for Giovanni di Paolo Rucellai by Leon Battista Alberti between 1446 and 1451, its facade among the first to apply classical orders to Renaissance architecture.

santa-maria-novella.name: Santa Maria Novella
santa-maria-novella.summary: A Dominican church in Florence, considered the most important Romano-Gothic church in Tuscany, built from 1290 and home to major Renaissance artworks by Giotto and Masaccio.

st-mark-s-basilica.name: St Mark's Basilica
st-mark-s-basilica.summary: The cathedral church of Venice, dedicated to Saint Mark and attached to the Doge's Palace; the current building was begun around 1063, modeled on a church in Constantinople.

lonja-de-la-seda.name: Silk Exchange of Valencia
lonja-de-la-seda.summary: A late Gothic civil building in Valencia, Spain, now a major tourist attraction.

frederick-barbarossa.name: Frederick Barbarossa
frederick-barbarossa.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 to 1190, also King of Germany, Italy and Burgundy; his Italian nickname "Barbarossa," meaning Red Beard, became one of history's most enduring monikers.

legnano.name: Legnano
legnano.summary: An Italian town near Milan, site of the 1176 battle where the Lombard League defeated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa; the only town besides Rome named in Italy's national anthem.

lombard-league.name: Lombard League
lombard-league.summary: An alliance of northern Italian cities formed in 1167, backed by the popes, to resist Holy Roman imperial control; it disbanded in 1250.

reconquista.name: Reconquista
reconquista.summary: A centuries-long series of military campaigns by Christian kingdoms in Iberia against Muslim-ruled al-Andalus, beginning around 718 to 722 and ending in 1492 with the capture of Granada.

isabella-i-of-castile.name: Isabella I of Castile
isabella-i-of-castile.summary: Queen of Castile and León from 1474 to 1504 and, with her husband Ferdinand II of Aragon, one of the Catholic Monarchs who completed the Reconquista and financed Columbus's 1492 voyage.

ferdinand-ii-of-aragon.name: Ferdinand II of Aragon
ferdinand-ii-of-aragon.summary: King of Aragon from 1479 and, through marriage to Isabella I, joint ruler of Castile as one of the Catholic Monarchs; together they sponsored Columbus's 1492 voyage and completed the Reconquista by conquering Granada.

crown-of-castile.name: Castile
crown-of-castile.summary: A medieval Iberian kingdom formed in 1230 by uniting Castile and León, joined to the Crown of Aragon in 1479 through royal marriage, and sponsor of Columbus's 1492 voyage.

carroccio.name: Carroccio
carroccio.summary: A large four-wheeled wagon carrying a medieval Italian city's religious and civic symbols, around which its militia gathered and fought; losing it in battle counted as a humiliating defeat.

henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Henry VII, Holy Roman Emperor
henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of Germany from 1308 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1312, the first of the House of Luxembourg, who ended the Great Interregnum but died suddenly while campaigning in Italy.

iron-crown.name: Iron Crown
iron-crown.summary: A medieval reliquary crown of gold and jewels around a central band traditionally said to be forged from a nail of the True Cross, used to crown some Holy Roman Emperors as kings of Italy.

kingdom-of-naples.name: Kingdom of Naples
kingdom-of-naples.summary: A state ruling southern Italy from 1282 to 1816, formed after the War of the Sicilian Vespers and later contested by France and Spain before coming under Spanish control by 1504.

duchy-of-milan.name: Duchy of Milan
duchy-of-milan.summary: A Northern Italian state created in 1395 by Gian Galeazzo Visconti, later prospering under the Sforza family's silk industry before falling to Napoleon's forces in 1796.

treaty-of-lodi.name: Treaty of Lodi
treaty-of-lodi.summary: Peace agreement signed in 1454 that ended the Wars in Lombardy between the Venetian Republic and the Duchy of Milan.

wars-in-lombardy.name: Wars in Lombardy
wars-in-lombardy.summary: A series of conflicts from 1423 to 1454 between Venice and Milan for dominance in northern Italy, ending with the Treaty of Lodi and reshaping Italy's political map.

italic-league.name: Italic League
italic-league.summary: An alliance formed in 1454 between the Papal States, Venice, Milan, Florence and Naples that kept peace and a balance of power in Italy for about 40 years.

lorenzo-de-medici.name: Lorenzo de' Medici
lorenzo-de-medici.summary: An Italian statesman (1449–1492), known as "the Magnificent," who was de facto ruler of Florence and the leading patron of Renaissance artists such as Botticelli and Michelangelo.

ludovico-sforza.name: Ludovico Sforza
ludovico-sforza.summary: Italian nobleman (1452–1508), called 'the Moor,' who ruled as Duke of Milan from 1494 to 1499 and became a great Renaissance art patron before dying imprisoned in France.

charles-viii-of-france.name: Charles VIII of France
charles-viii-of-france.summary: King of France from 1483 to 1498, called 'the Affable'; his marriage to Anne of Brittany brought Brittany into union with France, and he invaded Italy in 1494 with powerful new artillery.

italian-war-of-1494-1495.name: Italian War of 1494-95
italian-war-of-1494-1495.summary: The opening phase of the Italian Wars, pitting Charles VIII of France against the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, and an Italian alliance led by Pope Alexander VI known as the League of Venice.

pope-alexander-iii.name: Pope Alexander III
pope-alexander-iii.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1159 to 1181, who spent much of his reign outside Rome opposing rivals backed by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa; canonized Thomas Becket.

peace-of-constance.name: Peace of Constance
peace-of-constance.summary: An 1183 privilege granted by Emperor Frederick I to the Lombard League, permanently ending their conflict and recognizing extensive rights for the league's cities while preserving imperial authority.

alessandria.name: Alessandria
alessandria.summary: A city in Italy's Piedmont region and capital of its province, known for the Borsalino hat company and its proximity to the site of the Battle of Marengo.

francis-of-assisi.name: Francis of Assisi
francis-of-assisi.summary: Italian mystic, poet and friar (c. 1181–1226) who founded the Franciscan religious order after turning to a life of poverty; one of Christianity's most venerated figures.

canticle-of-the-sun.name: Canticle of the Sun
canticle-of-the-sun.summary: A religious song composed by Saint Francis of Assisi, written in an Umbrian Italian dialect and considered the first known-author work of literature in the Italian language.

dante-alighieri.name: Dante Alighieri
dante-alighieri.summary: Italian poet and philosopher (c. 1265–1321) famed for the Divine Comedy, and a pioneer of writing in vernacular Tuscan rather than Latin.

sicilian-school.name: Sicilian School
sicilian-school.summary: Community of poets at Frederick II's court in Palermo, led by Giacomo da Lentini, who produced over 300 courtly love poems between 1230 and 1266, marking the start of Sicilian-language literature.

cantigas-de-santa-maria.name: Cantigas de Santa Maria
cantigas-de-santa-maria.summary: A collection of 420 medieval songs with musical notation in Galician-Portuguese from the court of Alfonso X of Castile (1221-1284), mentioning the Virgin Mary in every verse.

alfonso-x-of-castile.name: Alfonso X of Castile
alfonso-x-of-castile.summary: King of Castile, León and Galicia from 1252 to 1284, nicknamed the Wise, who sponsored the Alfonsine astronomical tables and issued Castile's first law code written in the vernacular.

rustichello-da-pisa.name: Rustichello da Pisa
rustichello-da-pisa.summary: A late 13th-century Italian romance writer best known for co-writing Marco Polo's account of his travels while the two were imprisoned together in Genoa.

the-travels-of-marco-polo.name: The Travels of Marco Polo
the-travels-of-marco-polo.summary: A 13th-century travelogue written down by Rustichello da Pisa from stories told by Venetian explorer Marco Polo, describing his travels through Asia from 1271 to 1295 and his time at Kublai Khan's court.

giovanni-villani.name: Giovanni Villani
giovanni-villani.summary: A Florentine banker and official (c. 1276/1280–1348) who wrote the Nuova Cronica, a year-by-year chronicle of Florence and Europe, notable for its early use of statistics in history.

nuova-cronica.name: Nuova Cronica
nuova-cronica.summary: A 14th-century year-by-year history of Florence by Giovanni Villani, covering building projects, trade, and disasters, continued after his death by his brother and nephew.

filippo-villani.name: Filippo Villani
filippo-villani.summary: A Florentine chronicler active around 1400 who continued his family's Nuova Cronica, extending it down to 1364.

brunetto-latini.name: Brunetto Latini
brunetto-latini.summary: Italian philosopher, scholar, notary and statesman (c. 1220-1294) who was a teacher and friend of Dante Alighieri.

cicero.name: Cicero
cicero.summary: A Roman statesman, lawyer, philosopher and orator (106–43 BC) who served as consul in 63 BC and greatly shaped the Latin language through his surviving writings.

de-inventione.name: De Inventione
de-inventione.summary: An early handbook on rhetoric written by Cicero as a young man, credited with the first recorded use of the term 'liberal arts'.

martino-da-canal.name: Martino da Canal
martino-da-canal.summary: 13th-century Venetian chronicler whose only known work, Les estoires de Venise, is a French-language history of Venice up to 1275.

orosius.name: Orosius
orosius.summary: Roman priest, historian and theologian (c. 375/385 to c. 420), a student of Augustine of Hippo who collaborated with him on the City of God and wrote the history Seven Books Against the Pagans.

vegetius.name: Vegetius
vegetius.summary: A late 4th-century Roman writer known mainly through his military manual Epitoma rei militaris and a lesser-known guide to veterinary medicine; little else is known of his life.

de-re-militari.name: De re militari
de-re-militari.summary: A Latin treatise on Roman warfare and military methods, written by Vegetius in the 5th century CE, that became an influential military guide throughout the Middle Ages and beyond.

marsilius-of-padua.name: Marsilius of Padua
marsilius-of-padua.summary: Italian scholar (c. 1275–1342) whose treatise Defensor Pacis attacked papal claims to power over church and state, making him a forerunner of the Protestant Reformation.

louis-iv-holy-roman-emperor.name: Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor
louis-iv-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of the Romans from 1314 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1328 to 1347, whose disputed election led to war with his Habsburg rival and conflict with Pope John XXII.

dino-compagni.name: Dino Compagni
dino-compagni.summary: Italian writer and political figure (c. 1255–1324), active in Florentine government, who wrote the Cronica, a history of Florence covering 1280 to 1312.

andrea-da-grosseto.name: Andrea da Grosseto
andrea-da-grosseto.summary: An Italian writer active in the 13th century.

albertanus-of-brescia.name: Albertanus of Brescia
albertanus-of-brescia.summary: Author of Latin social treatises and sermons, active in Brescia, Italy, c. 1195 to c. 1251.

aldebrandin-of-siena.name: Aldebrandin of Siena
aldebrandin-of-siena.summary: Italian physician (died 1296/1299?) who lived in Siena and Troyes and wrote the 1256 sanitation guidebook Le Régime du corps.

beatrice-of-savoy.name: Beatrice of Savoy
beatrice-of-savoy.summary: Countess consort of Provence (c. 1198-c. 1267) through marriage to Ramon Berenguer V, and later regent of her native Savoy.

umayyad-state-of-c-rdoba.name: Caliphate of Córdoba
umayyad-state-of-c-rdoba.summary: Arab Islamic state ruled by the Umayyad dynasty in Iberia from 756 to 1031, first as an emirate and from 929 as a caliphate, with its capital at Córdoba becoming a centre of trade and learning.

abbadid-dynasty.name: Abbadid dynasty
abbadid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty that ruled the Taifa of Seville from about 1023 to 1091 after the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba, becoming the most powerful of the Taifa kingdoms.

university-of-bologna.name: University of Bologna
university-of-bologna.summary: The oldest continuously operating university in the world, teaching since around 1088 in Bologna, Italy, and a major center of Renaissance science that educated Copernicus.

university-of-salamanca.name: University of Salamanca
university-of-salamanca.summary: Founded in 1218 by King Alfonso IX, the oldest university in the Hispanic world and the fourth-oldest continuously operating university in the world.

al-zarqali.name: Al-Zarqali
al-zarqali.summary: An Arab maker of astronomical instruments and astrologer (1029–1100) from al-Andalus, inventor of a perfected astrolabe used by navigators for centuries.

adelard-of-bath.name: Adelard of Bath
adelard-of-bath.summary: 12th-century English natural philosopher who translated major Greek scientific works, including the first Latin translation of Euclid's Elements, from Arabic into Latin, helping introduce Arabic numerals to Europe.

euclid-s-elements.name: Euclid's Elements
euclid-s-elements.summary: A mathematical treatise written around 300 BC by Euclid, gathering definitions, constructions and theorems in 13 books; often called the most successful textbook ever written.

roger-ii-of-sicily.name: Roger II of Sicily
roger-ii-of-sicily.summary: Roger II of Sicily: King of Sicily from 1130 and King of Africa from 1148, both until his death in 1154, who began his rule as Count of Sicily in 1105 and became Duke of Apulia and Calabria in 1127.

tabula-rogeriana.name: Tabula Rogeriana
tabula-rogeriana.summary: An atlas of the known world commissioned by Norman King Roger II and completed by geographer al-Idrisi in 1154, compiling 70 maps with commentary.

signoria.name: Signore
signoria.summary: Italian for "lord," the title of the ruling authority (signoria) that governed many medieval and Renaissance Italian city-states.

investiture-controversy.name: Investiture Controversy
investiture-controversy.summary: An 11th- and 12th-century conflict between the Church and Holy Roman Emperors over who could appoint bishops and abbots, lasting nearly 50 years until the 1122 Concordat of Worms.

battle-of-legnano.name: Battle of Legnano
battle-of-legnano.summary: 1176 battle in which infantry of the Lombard League, led by Milan, defeated the cavalry of Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, a major setback in his long conflict with the Italian cities and the Pope.

siege-and-battle-of-parma.name: Siege and Battle of Parma (1248)
siege-and-battle-of-parma.summary: A 1247–48 siege by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II against the rebel city of Parma that ended when the Parmesans stormed and destroyed his fortified camp of Vittoria, a serious setback for Frederick.

gian-galeazzo-visconti.name: Gian Galeazzo Visconti
gian-galeazzo-visconti.summary: First duke of Milan from 1395, who ruled Lombardy, conquered territory in the Po Valley, and founded the Certosa di Pavia before dying of fever in 1402.

wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia.name: Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia
wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia.summary: King of Bohemia from 1378 to 1419 and King of the Romans and Germany from 1376 to 1400, nicknamed the Idle.

manuel-i-komnenos.name: Manuel I Komnenos
manuel-i-komnenos.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1118 to 1180 who pursued an ambitious foreign policy, allied with the papacy, invaded Norman Sicily, and extended Byzantine influence over Hungary and the Crusader states.

hastings-rashdall.name: Hastings Rashdall
hastings-rashdall.summary: English philosopher, theologian, historian and Anglican priest (1858–1924), a major historian of medieval universities known for the theory of ideal utilitarianism.

anselm-of-canterbury.name: Anselm of Canterbury
anselm-of-canterbury.summary: Benedictine abbot, philosopher and theologian who served as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109; credited as originator of the ontological argument for God's existence.

ontological-argument.name: Ontological argument
ontological-argument.summary: Type of philosophical argument for God's existence based purely on reasoning about being, first proposed in the West by Anselm of Canterbury in 1078.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

thomas-aquinas.name: Thomas Aquinas
thomas-aquinas.summary: An Italian Dominican friar, theologian and philosopher (c. 1225–1274) who blended Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine and founded the school of thought called Thomism.

thomism.name: Thomism
thomism.summary: The philosophical and theological school built on the work of Thomas Aquinas, whose writings remain central to Catholic philosophy and theology.

dominican-order.name: Dominican Order
dominican-order.summary: Catholic mendicant order, also called the Order of Preachers, founded in France by Dominic de Guzmán and approved by Pope Honorius III in 1216; known for its intellectual tradition.

dominic-de-guzm-n.name: St Dominic
dominic-de-guzm-n.summary: Castilian priest (1170 to 1221) who founded the Order of Preachers, known as the Dominicans, and is the patron saint of astronomers and natural scientists.

albertus-magnus.name: Albertus Magnus
albertus-magnus.summary: German Dominican friar, philosopher, scientist and bishop (c. 1200–1280), considered one of the greatest medieval thinkers and canonized in 1931.

william-of-moerbeke.name: William of Moerbeke
william-of-moerbeke.summary: William of Moerbeke: 13th-century translator who rendered Greek philosophical, medical and scientific texts into Latin; his translations were influential and are still respected by modern scholars.

gemistos-plethon.name: Gemistos Plethon
gemistos-plethon.summary: A Greek scholar and philosopher of the late Byzantine era (c. 1355-1454) who reintroduced Plato's ideas to Western Europe at the Council of Florence and helped spark the Florentine Renaissance.

julius-pomponius-laetus.name: Pomponio Leto
julius-pomponius-laetus.summary: Italian humanist, also known as Giulio Pomponio Leto, who lived from 1428 to 1498.

pope-paul-ii.name: Pope Paul II
pope-paul-ii.summary: Head of the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1464 to 1471, an art and antiquities collector who rose quickly through the Church after his uncle became pope.

pontifex-maximus.name: Pontifex Maximus
pontifex-maximus.summary: The chief high priest of ancient Rome's College of Pontiffs; originally a religious post, it grew increasingly political and was absorbed into the role of emperor beginning with Augustus.

commercial-revolution.name: Commercial revolution
commercial-revolution.summary: The growth of a European trade-based economy from the 11th century, spurred by Crusades-era demand for spices and silks, until the Industrial Revolution; marked by rising banking, insurance and investment.

pope-boniface-viii.name: Pope Boniface VIII
pope-boniface-viii.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1294 to 1303, who made strong claims to papal power and clashed with the kings of France and Germany; established the first Catholic jubilee year.

jubilee-in-the-catholic-church.name: Papal Jubilee
jubilee-in-the-catholic-church.summary: A special year of remission of sins and universal pardon in Catholic tradition, dating to 1300 when Pope Boniface VIII convoked the first such holy year, marked by pilgrimage to Rome.

central_asia_steppe-medieval-art-005: Church of San Francesco in Assisi
